report:
## Does Magnesium Supplementation Improve Depression Symptoms?

The evidence is mixed and of generally low quality, so a firm "no" is too strong — but claims of proven benefit are overstated.

**Supportive findings:** A widely cited 2017 open-label RCT (Tarleton et al., *PLoS One*) found that 248 mg/day of magnesium chloride for 6 weeks modestly improved depressive symptoms in adults with mild-to-moderate depression, though the trial lacked a placebo control and had high attrition. A 2023 meta-analysis (Frontiers in Psychiatry, PMC10783196) pooling 8 effect sizes from RCTs reported a statistically significant reduction in depression scores (SMD ≈ -0.92), but the authors noted substantial heterogeneity, small sample sizes, short duration, and variable magnesium doses/forms across included trials — factors that undermine confidence in the pooled result (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10783196/; https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/psychiatry/articles/10.3389/fpsyt.2023.1333261/full).

**Weaker/mixed findings:** A systematic review and meta-analysis in *BJPsych Open* examining magnesium and mood disorders found that dietary magnesium intake was inversely associated with depression only in cross-sectional studies, not in prospective cohort studies — suggesting reverse causation or confounding rather than a true protective effect (https://www.cambridge.org/core/journals/bjpsych-open/article/magnesium-and-mood-disorders-systematic-review-and-metaanalysis/9257DB9E4EAC7F0A5C5B84E63B4D3AEF).

**Conclusion:** Most existing trials are small, short, often unblinded, and heterogeneous in magnesium dose/form and population (many recruiting people with low baseline magnesium). While some studies and pooled analyses show statistically significant improvement, the overall evidence base is not robust enough to confirm a genuine antidepressant effect for the general population. Magnesium may help specifically in magnesium-deficient individuals, but it is not established as an effective standalone depression treatment. Larger, well-controlled trials are needed before drawing firm conclusions.
